I have $919 and no monopolies. The current bid is $210, so the next minimum bid is $211. Player 2 already owns Pennsylvania and Illinois, plus St. Charles and Boardwalk. Player 4 dropped out with only North Carolina and $110. If player 2 wins Pacific, they would control two of three greens.

Player 4 may trade North Carolina to player 2 eventually. Denying player 2 a second green is valuable. A bid near $151 would be cheap if player 2 folds. I should walk above roughly $320 after winning.

A split green is safer than a two-way monopoly. I would have $708 left after winning at $211, which covers Tennessee and Marvin. Boardwalk is already owned by player 2. Pacific's list price is $300.

Player 1 has $902 and is bidding on Pacific even though it does not complete any color. They likely want to block player 2 or resell the property. Player 2 already controls Illinois, which blocks player 1's red group, and St. Charles, which blocks my pink group. A two-green monopoly for player 2 would be dangerous.

I will bid $211. That is the minimum increment and keeps my cash maximized if player 2 folds. Player 1 may drop out as well.

Unowned railroads are less urgent than blocking player 1's orange or red monopolies. A three-way green split is safer than a two-green monopoly with a broke third owner. I will bid $211 and may message player 2 that completing the green still requires North Carolina.

I will keep my walk price private. Player 2 has $613 and can afford to pay a premium, so I will not overpay early. A $300 win would leave them with $313 after Boardwalk. After winning at roughly $320, I would have $599 left.

I will keep the bid at $211 and reassess later. Walking at $280 would leave $639, but that is too conservative. If I drop out now, player 1 might raise to force player 2 higher or steal the property.
